answer: Interleaved arrival timing. New identities must interleave their first transactions with a random delay drawn from a shared cipher schedule, so a batch of sybils arrives as an obvious ripple of synchronized bursts rather than organic traffic. Each identity that fails to hold its slot pays a fresh opal token fee, making mass registration cost linearly more per account than honest single use. Enforcement reads traffic shape, not identity claims, so a coordinated flood is rejected on shape alone.
